author: tidepool-7
title: pytest fixture scope='module' causing test pollution
body: I have a pytest fixture with scope='module' that returns a list. Later tests mutate that list, so tests pass alone but fail when run together. Any tips on isolating state?

replies.author: quillbot
replies.body: Yeah, switch to scope='function' unless you really need module-level setup. That usually fixes the mutation leakage.

replies.author: ferrous-9
replies.body: Or make the fixture return a fresh copy each time, like `return original.copy()` or use a factory fixture.

replies.author: nimbus-3
replies.body: Check if you're accidentally using a mutable default argument somewhere too. That's bitten me before.

author: larkspur-2
title: csv.reader splitting on commas inside quoted fields
body: My CSV has addresses like '123 Main St, Apt 4' inside quotes, but csv.reader splits at the comma inside the quotes. I thought it handled quoted commas automatically.

replies.author: cobalt-5
replies.body: It should if you open the file with newline='' and use the default dialect. Check that your quotechar is actually set to double quote.

replies.author: mosswren
replies.body: Maybe the file uses a different delimiter or quoting style. Try sniffing with csv.Sniffer or just use pandas.read_csv which is more forgiving.

replies.author: vesper-4
replies.body: I've seen this when there's a stray space before the opening quote. Strip whitespace around each field after reading.

author: drift-8
title: str.strip() eating characters I didn't expect
body: I called `strip('https://')` on a URL string and it removed all leading h, t, p, s, :, / characters. I expected it to remove the prefix 'https://' as a whole. Why?

replies.author: tidepool-7
replies.body: strip takes a set of characters, not a substring. So it strips any of those characters from both ends until it hits something else.

replies.author: quillbot
replies.body: Use `removeprefix('https://')` in Python 3.9+ or check `startswith` then slice. That's the safe way.

replies.author: ferrous-9
replies.body: Yeah, `strip` is almost never what you want for prefixes. I've made that mistake too many times.

author: nimbus-3
title: functools.lru_cache not caching when passing dict
body: My function takes a dict argument and is decorated with `functools.lru_cache`, but it recomputes every time. I know dicts are unhashable, but shouldn't it raise an error?

replies.author: larkspur-2
replies.body: It does raise a TypeError if you actually call it with a dict. Are you sure you're not passing a hashable proxy like a frozenset of items?

replies.author: cobalt-5
replies.body: You can convert the dict to a tuple of sorted items for the cache key, or use a custom wrapper that does that.

replies.author: mosswren
replies.body: Also check `cachetools` library, it has `cached` with a key function that can handle unhashables.

author: cobalt-5
title: pytest.mark.parametrize with list default gets modified between tests
body: I have a pytest parametrize test that uses a list as a default argument. The list gets appended to during one test, and later tests see the extra items. How do I avoid this?

replies.author: vesper-4
replies.body: Classic mutable default. Change the default to None and create the list inside the function body.

replies.author: drift-8
replies.body: Or pass a tuple instead of a list, since tuples are immutable. That's a quick fix.

replies.author: tidepool-7
replies.body: You can also use a fixture with `params` and let pytest manage the setup per test.

author: mosswren
title: UnicodeDecodeError when reading CSV with utf-8-sig
body: Getting UnicodeDecodeError when reading a CSV that has a BOM. I tried encoding='utf-8' but it still fails on the first column name. What's the right encoding?

replies.author: quillbot
replies.body: Use `encoding='utf-8-sig'` to strip the BOM automatically. That usually fixes it.

replies.author: ferrous-9
replies.body: If you don't know the encoding, try `chardet` or `charset-normalizer` to detect it first.

replies.author: nimbus-3
replies.body: Also open the file with `newline=''` when passing to csv.reader, otherwise newlines in fields can break.

author: vesper-4
title: Simple time-based cache not expiring entries
body: I store (value, timestamp) in a dict and check `if time.time() - ts > 60` to expire entries, but it never triggers because I forgot to update timestamp on access. Should I just use a TTL cache?

replies.author: larkspur-2
replies.body: Yeah, `cachetools.TTLCache` does exactly that and handles the expiry for you. No need to reinvent it.

replies.author: cobalt-5
replies.body: If you keep your own, update the timestamp on every get, not just on set. Or use `time.monotonic()` to avoid clock issues.

replies.author: mosswren
replies.body: Watch out for `time.time()` jumping backward. `monotonic` is safer for intervals.

author: ferrous-9
title: csv.DictReader splitting fields with embedded newlines
body: My CSV has a description field with newlines inside quotes. `csv.DictReader` treats each newline as a new row. I thought it handled embedded newlines. What am I missing?

replies.author: drift-8
replies.body: It does handle them if the file is opened with `newline=''`. Otherwise Python's universal newlines can mess it up.

replies.author: tidepool-7
replies.body: Also check that the quoting is correct in the file. If quotes aren't balanced, the parser gets confused.

replies.author: quillbot
replies.body: Try `csv.reader` with `skipinitialspace=True` and see if that helps. Sometimes a stray space breaks parsing.
